questions.question: What are the most important String methods you should know for interviews?
questions.title: Most Important String Methods in Java
questions.direct_answer: The must-know String methods for interviews: `length()`, `charAt(i)`, `substring(start, end)`, `indexOf(str)`, `contains(str)`, `startsWith()`/`endsWith()`, `equals()`/`equalsIgnoreCase()`, `toLowerCase()`/`toUpperCase()`, `trim()`/`strip()`, `replace(old, new)`, `split(regex)`, and `String.valueOf(x)` / `Integer.parseInt(s)` for type conversion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the practical String API well enough to use it in a coding problem without hesitation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that String methods return a new String — calling s.toUpperCase() without assigning the result is a no-op. Also confusing length() (method, needs parentheses) with array's length (field, no parentheses).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java 11 added strip(), isBlank(), and lines() — strip() is Unicode-aware while trim() only removes ASCII whitespace (char <= 32).

sections.title: The 15 Methods That Cover 90% of Real String Code
sections.content:
A **String method** is a built-in operation you call on a piece of text — to measure it, search inside it, compare it, or produce a changed copy of it.

The `String` class ships **over 60 methods**, but day-to-day code and interviews lean on roughly 15. The thing that makes you fast in a coding round isn't knowing all 60 — it's knowing exactly what these 15 return and what their index rules are, so you never pause mid-solution.

The easiest way to hold them in your head is by **purpose**:
- **Access** — `length()`, `charAt(i)`
- **Search** — `indexOf()`, `contains()`, `startsWith()`/`endsWith()`
- **Compare** — `equals()`, `equalsIgnoreCase()`
- **Transform** — `toUpperCase()`/`toLowerCase()`, `trim()`/`strip()`, `replace()`
- **Extract** — `substring()`, `split()`
- **Convert** — `String.valueOf()`, `Integer.parseInt()`

Three rules cut across all of them. First, because `String` is **immutable**, every method returns a *new* String — `s.toUpperCase()` on its own line does nothing; you must capture the result. Second, `length()` is a **method** with parentheses, unlike an array's `length` field — a constant fresher trip-up. Third, indices are **0-based** and any `start`/`end` pair uses an **exclusive** end, so `end - start` is the length.

The gotcha that separates real experience from textbook reading: `trim()` only strips characters with code `≤ 32`, so a Unicode non-breaking space survives it. Java 11 added `strip()` (Unicode-aware), `isBlank()`, and `lines()` — in modern code, prefer `strip()`.

sections.title: The Six Jobs the Core String Methods Do
sections.content:
Grouping the methods by what they are *for* makes them far easier to recall under pressure than a flat alphabetical list. ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Core String methods"] --> A["Access"] S --> SE["Search"] S --> CP["Compare"] S --> T["Transform → new String"] S --> X["Extract"] S --> CV["Convert"] A --> A1["length()
charAt(i)"] SE --> SE1["indexOf()
contains()
startsWith() / endsWith()"] CP --> CP1["equals()
equalsIgnoreCase()"] T --> T1["toUpperCase() / toLowerCase()
trim() / strip()
replace()"] X --> X1["substring()
split()"] CV --> CV1["String.valueOf()
Integer.parseInt()"] ``` Notice the **Transform** branch is labelled "new String" — none of those mutate the original. That single fact is behind the most common String bug freshers hit.

sections.title: The Core 15 Methods — All in One Place
String Methods Quick Reference
sections.content:
| Method | Returns | Key note |
|---|---|---|
| `length()` | `int` | Method — needs `()`, unlike `array.length` |
| `charAt(i)` | `char` | 0-based index |
| `substring(start)` | `String` | From start to end of string |
| `substring(start, end)` | `String` | end is exclusive |
| `indexOf(str)` | `int` | -1 if not found |
| `contains(str)` | `boolean` | Case-sensitive |
| `startsWith(prefix)` | `boolean` | Case-sensitive |
| `endsWith(suffix)` | `boolean` | Case-sensitive |
| `equals(other)` | `boolean` | Content comparison — use instead of == |
| `equalsIgnoreCase(other)` | `boolean` | Case-insensitive content comparison |
| `toUpperCase()` | `String` | New String — assign the result |
| `toLowerCase()` | `String` | New String — assign the result |
| `trim()` | `String` | Removes ASCII whitespace (char ≤ 32) |
| `strip()` | `String` | Java 11 — removes Unicode whitespace |
| `replace(old, new)` | `String` | Replaces all occurrences |
| `split(regex)` | `String[]` | Splits by regex pattern |
| `String.valueOf(x)` | `String` | Converts any primitive/object to String |
| `isEmpty()` | `boolean` | True if length == 0 |
| `isBlank()` | `boolean` | Java 11 — true if empty or only whitespace |

sections.title: The Traps That Bite Every Java Fresher
sections.content:
- **Calling a transform without using the return value** — `s.trim();` on its own line does nothing, because `String` is immutable. You must write `s = s.trim();`. This is the single most common String bug for beginners.
- **Writing `s.length` instead of `s.length()`** — `String` exposes a *method*, arrays expose a *field*. Mixing them up is a compile error, and it goes the other way too: `arr.length()` doesn't compile either.
- **Using `trim()` on Unicode whitespace** — `trim()` only removes characters with code `≤ 32`, so a non-breaking space (`\u00A0`) survives it and your "empty" check passes when it shouldn't. Use `strip()` (Java 11+).
- **Feeding `indexOf()`'s `-1` straight into another call** — `s.charAt(s.indexOf("x"))` or `s.substring(s.indexOf("x"))` throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` when the substring is absent. Always check for `-1` first.
- **Comparing text with `==` instead of `equals()`** — `==` compares object references, not characters, so two strings with identical content can return `false`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Every method returns a new String** — `s.toUpperCase()` on its own line is a no-op; immutability means you must capture the result with `s = s.toUpperCase()`.
- **`length()` is a method, `array.length` is a field** — `s.length` or `arr.length()` is a compile error; the inconsistency trips up freshers constantly.
- **`substring(start, end)` end is exclusive** — `"hello".substring(1, 3)` returns `"el"`, not `"ell"`; `end - start` equals the result length.
- **`indexOf()` returns `-1` when not found** — never feed that into `charAt()` or `substring()` or you get `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
- **`strip()` beats `trim()` since Java 11** — `trim()` only removes chars with code `≤ 32`, so a Unicode non-breaking space survives; `strip()` is Unicode-aware.
- **`equals()` compares content, `==` compares references** — use `equals()`/`equalsIgnoreCase()` for text; `==` can return `false` for identical characters.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd group them rather than rattle off a list. For access there's `length()` and `charAt()`; for searching, `indexOf()`, `contains()`, and `startsWith()`/`endsWith()`; for comparing, `equals()` and `equalsIgnoreCase()`; for transforming, `toUpperCase()`, `trim()`/`strip()`, and `replace()`; and for extracting, `substring()` and `split()`. Conversion goes `String.valueOf()` one way and `Integer.parseInt()` the other.

The thing I always stress is that `String` is **immutable**, so every one of these returns a new String — writing `s.toUpperCase();` on its own line changes nothing, you have to assign the result back. That's the bug I see most often. And `length()` is a method with parentheses, unlike an array's `length` field; that inconsistency catches people out both ways.

A detail that shows you've kept up with the language: Java 11 added `strip()`, `isBlank()`, and `lines()`. `strip()` is **Unicode-aware** where `trim()` only removes ASCII whitespace up to code 32 — so a non-breaking space survives `trim()` but not `strip()`. In modern code I default to `strip()`, and I check existence with `indexOf()` returning `-1` before I ever use that result as an index.

questions.question: How does String.format() work and when do you use it?
questions.title: String.format() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `String.format(template, args...)` returns a formatted String by replacing placeholders in the template with provided values. Common placeholders: `%s` for strings, `%d` for integers, `%f` for floating-point, `%n` for newline. It is used when you need readable, structured string output — especially for reports, log messages, or display strings.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the format specifier syntax and can use String.format() for readable output construction.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using + concatenation for multi-value messages when String.format() would be clearer. Also mixing up %s (any object, calls toString) and %d (must be integer — throws exception for String).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java 15 introduced text blocks (triple-quoted strings) as an alternative for multi-line templates, and that printf() is String.format() but printed directly to System.out.

sections.title: Templates Over Glue: Why format() Beats String Concatenation
sections.content:
`String.format()` builds a string by taking a **template** and dropping your values into placeholder slots like `%s` and `%d`.

It exists because `+` concatenation falls apart for multi-value messages. A log line built by gluing fragments — `"User " + name + " logged in at " + time + " from " + ip` — is hard to read and easy to break (forget a space, misorder a fragment). The same thing as a template reads as one sentence: `String.format("User %s logged in at %s from %s", name, time, ip)`. It's Java's equivalent of Python's f-strings or C's `printf`.

How it works: each placeholder is filled by the next argument **in order**. The specifiers you'll actually use:
- `%s` — any object; calls `.toString()`, so it never throws on type
- `%d` — integer (`int`, `long`) only
- `%f` — floating-point; `%.2f` rounds to 2 decimals
- `%n` — a platform-independent newline
- `%10s` right-aligns in a 10-wide field; `%-10s` left-aligns

The nuance worth knowing: `%s` is lenient, but `%d` is strict — hand it a `double` or a `String` and you get an `IllegalFormatConversionException` at **runtime**, not compile time. The gotcha freshers hit is using `\n` inside a template instead of `%n`, and expecting `%f` to print cleanly — bare `%f` always shows 6 decimals (`3.140000`). To stand out, mention that `printf()` is just `format()` printed directly, that Java 15 added text blocks for multi-line templates, and that `"...".formatted(args)` is the newer instance-method shortcut.

sections.title: How a Template and Its Arguments Become One String
sections.content:
`String.format()` walks the template left to right, and each placeholder consumes the next argument in order. ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Template
'Name: %s, Age: %d'"] --> F["String.format()"] A["Arguments
'Alice', 28"] --> F F --> R["Result
'Name: Alice, Age: 28'"] ``` Because matching is **positional**, the count and order of arguments must line up with the placeholders. Too few arguments throws `MissingFormatArgumentException`; a type mismatch like `%d` against a `double` throws `IllegalFormatConversionException`.

sections.title: String.format() in Practice
Common Format Specifiers
sections.content:
| Specifier | Type | Example | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%s` | Any object | `format("%s", "hello")` | `hello` |
| `%d` | int / long | `format("%d", 42)` | `42` |
| `%f` | float / double | `format("%f", 3.14)` | `3.140000` |
| `%.2f` | float / double | `format("%.2f", 3.14159)` | `3.14` |
| `%b` | boolean | `format("%b", true)` | `true` |
| `%c` | char | `format("%c", 'A')` | `A` |
| `%n` | newline | `format("line1%nline2")` | line1 + newline + line2 |
| `%10s` | right-pad | `format("%10s", "hi")` | `        hi` |
| `%-10s` | left-pad | `format("%-10s", "hi")` | `hi        ` |

sections.title: Where format() Blows Up at Runtime
sections.content:
- **Passing a non-integer to `%d`** — `String.format("%d", 3.14)` throws `IllegalFormatConversionException` at *runtime*, not compile time, so it sails through your build and fails in production. Use `%f` for decimals, or `%s` when the type is uncertain.
- **Mismatching the argument count** — too few arguments for the placeholders throws `MissingFormatArgumentException`; the compiler can't catch it because the template is just a String.
- **Using `\n` instead of `%n` in a template** — `%n` emits the platform line separator, while a hardcoded `\n` produces the wrong line ending for Windows-style consumers and log parsers.
- **Expecting `%f` to print clean decimals** — bare `%f` always prints 6 digits (`3.140000`); use `%.2f` to control precision for prices and scores.
- **Reaching for `+` on multi-value messages** — concatenation is harder to read, easy to misorder, and painful to localize compared to a single template.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`%s` works on any object** — it calls `toString()`, so it never throws on type; the safe default when you're unsure.
- **`%d` accepts integers only** — passing a `double` or `String` throws `IllegalFormatConversionException` at runtime, not compile time.
- **`%.2f` controls precision** — bare `%f` always prints 6 decimals (`3.140000`); use `%.2f` for prices and scores.
- **`%n` over `\n` in templates** — `%n` emits the platform line separator; a hardcoded `\n` is wrong on Windows.
- **`System.out.printf()` is `format()` + print** — same specifiers, nothing to assign; use it for console output.
- **Java 15 adds `"...".formatted(args)`** — an instance-method shortcut that reads cleaner than the static `String.format()`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I reach for `String.format()` whenever a message has several moving parts and `+` concatenation would turn into an unreadable chain. You write the sentence once with placeholders and pass the values in order — `String.format("User %s logged in from %s", name, ip)` reads far better than gluing five fragments together, and it's much easier to change later.

The placeholders worth knowing: `%s` for any object — it just calls `toString()`, so it's the safe one; `%d` strictly for integers; and `%.2f` for a double rounded to two places, which I use for money and scores. One real gotcha is that `%d` is checked at **runtime**, not compile time — hand it a `double` or a `String` and you get an `IllegalFormatConversionException` in production, so when the type is uncertain I default to `%s`. Inside templates I use `%n` rather than `\n` so the newline is **platform-correct**.

`printf()` is the same thing printed straight to the console, and since Java 15 there's `"Hello %s".formatted(name)` as a cleaner instance-method version. For anything beyond trivial gluing, I'd always pick a format template over concatenation.

questions.question: Why is the end index in String.substring() exclusive in Java?
questions.title: Why substring() End Index Is Exclusive
questions.direct_answer: In `String.substring(start, end)`, the `end` index is **exclusive** — the character at index `end` is not included. This convention is consistent across Java's entire standard library (`String.substring()`, `Arrays.copyOfRange()`, `List.subList()`, `String.split()`) and makes length calculation trivial: `end - start` always equals the resulting string's length.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the convention and can quickly calculate correct indices without off-by-one errors.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using the last character's index as end — e.g. substring(0, 4) on 'hello' gives 'hell' not 'hello'. To include index 4 you need substring(0, 5).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: The exclusive-end convention comes from Dijkstra's 1982 paper 'Why numbering should start at zero' — he showed that half-open intervals [start, end) give the nicest arithmetic: no ±1 adjustments, no edge cases at boundaries.

sections.title: Half-Open Intervals: Why end - start Always Equals the Length
sections.content:
`substring(start, end)` returns the slice of a string from index `start` up to — but **not including** — index `end`. So `"hello".substring(1, 3)` is `"el"`: positions 1 and 2, never 3.

This isn't arbitrary. The reason the end is exclusive is that it makes the arithmetic clean: `end - start` is **exactly** the length of what you get back, with no ±1 adjustment anywhere. Want the first five characters? `substring(0, 5)` — and 5 − 0 = 5.

How it generalizes: this is the **half-open interval** `[start, end)`, and Java uses it across almost every range API, so once it clicks it transfers:
- `String.substring(start, end)`
- `Arrays.copyOfRange(arr, from, to)`
- `List.subList(from, to)`

The nuance that makes the design pay off: adjacent ranges **tile perfectly**. Split a string into `substring(0, 5)` and `substring(5, 10)` and no character is counted twice and none is skipped — the shared boundary `5` belongs to the second slice only.

The gotcha everyone hits once: `"hello".substring(0, 4)` expecting the whole word, and getting `"hell"`. To include the last character you go *one past* its index, so `substring(0, 5)` — or just `substring(0, s.length())` for the whole string. It feels strange that you can legally pass `length()` as an index, but that's the half-open design. To stand out, note this is the same idea Dijkstra argued for in his 1982 note *"Why numbering should start at zero"* — half-open ranges give the nicest arithmetic with no edge cases at the boundaries.

sections.title: Index Map for "hello" — What Each Position Points To
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR I0["index 0
'h'"] --- I1["index 1
'e'"] --- I2["index 2
'l'"] --- I3["index 3
'l'"] --- I4["index 4
'o'"] ``` - `substring(1, 3)` → `"el"` — includes index 1, 2; excludes 3 - `substring(0, 5)` → `"hello"` — includes index 0–4; end = length = 5 - `substring(2)` → `"llo"` — from index 2 to the end (single-arg form)

sections.title: substring() Indices in Practice
The Off-by-One Errors substring() Invites
sections.content:
- **Using the last character's index as `end`** — `"hello".substring(0, 4)` returns `"hell"`, not `"hello"`. To include index 4 you need `end = 5`, one past the last character.
- **Forgetting `end` can equal `length()`** — `substring(0, s.length())` is perfectly legal and returns the whole string. `s.length()` is the one index you can pass that doesn't point at a real character.
- **Passing `end > length()` or `start < 0`** — both throw `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. `end` may *equal* the length but never exceed it.
- **Swapping the arguments** — `start > end` throws the same exception even when both numbers are individually in range.
- **Assuming `substring()` is free** — since Java 7u6 it allocates a fresh backing array, so on a hot path that slices a huge string repeatedly you pay a real copy cost each call (older JDKs shared the parent array and leaked it instead).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **End index is exclusive** — `substring(1, 3)` returns positions 1 and 2 only; the char at `end` is never included.
- **`end - start` is the result length** — want 5 chars from index 2? `substring(2, 7)`; no ±1 arithmetic.
- **`end` may equal `length()`** — `substring(0, s.length())` returns the whole string; that's the one out-of-range-looking index that's legal.
- **`substring(0, 4)` on `"hello"` gives `"hell"`** — the classic off-by-one; use `substring(0, 5)` or `substring(0, s.length())` for the whole word.
- **Same convention library-wide** — `Arrays.copyOfRange()` and `List.subList()` use half-open `[start, end)`, so adjacent slices tile with no overlap or gap.
- **Bad indices throw** — `start < 0`, `end > length()`, or `start > end` all raise `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The character at the `end` index isn't included — `substring(start, end)` gives you everything from `start` up to `end` minus one. So `"hello".substring(1, 3)` is `"el"`, just positions 1 and 2.

The reason this is worth internalizing is the **arithmetic** it buys you. Because the interval is half-open, `end - start` is exactly the length of what you get back — if I want five characters starting at index 2, that's `substring(2, 7)`, no off-by-one fiddling. Adjacent slices also **tile perfectly**: `substring(0, 5)` and `substring(5, 10)` share no character and leave no gap. Java uses this same `[start, end)` convention everywhere — `Arrays.copyOfRange()`, `List.subList()` — so once it clicks, it transfers.

The mistake everyone makes once is `"hello".substring(0, 4)` expecting the whole word and getting `"hell"`. To include the last character you go one past its index — `substring(0, 5)` — or just `substring(0, s.length())`. It feels odd that you can pass `length()` as an index, but that's the half-open design, and it's the same reasoning Dijkstra gave for why numbering should start at zero. When I want the rest of a string, I always reach for `s.length()` as the end.

questions.question: How does String.split() work and what are the common pitfalls?
questions.title: String.split() in Java — How It Works and Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: `String.split(regex)` splits the string around matches of the given regular expression and returns a `String[]`. The argument is a **regex**, not a plain string — special characters like `.`, `|`, `+`, `*`, `?` must be escaped. By default, trailing empty strings are removed from the result.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know that split() takes a regex, understand the escaping requirement for special chars, and know the trailing-empty-string behaviour.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling split('.') to split by dot — period is a regex metacharacter that matches ANY character. Every character becomes a delimiter and you get an array of empty strings. Must use split('\\.') to escape.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the two-arg form split(regex, limit) — with limit -1 it keeps trailing empty strings; with a positive limit it caps the number of pieces. Also: Java 8 added String.join() as the inverse operation.

sections.title: split() Takes a Regex — and That's Where the Bugs Live
sections.content:
`split()` breaks a String into an array of smaller strings wherever it finds a separator you specify.

That's the part everyone knows. The part that causes the bugs: **the separator is a regular expression**, not a literal string. You use it constantly — parsing CSV rows, file paths, query params, tokens — and most of the time it just works, because a comma or a space has no special meaning in regex, so `split(",")` and `split(" ")` behave exactly as you'd expect.

The trouble starts with characters that *are* **regex metacharacters**:
- `.` means "any character"
- `|` means "or"
- `+`, `*`, `?` are quantifiers
- `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`, `^`, `$` all carry special meaning

Split `"a.b.c"` with `split(".")` and you do *not* get `["a", "b", "c"]`. The `.` matches every character, so every position is a delimiter — you get back an empty array. The fix is to escape it: `split("\\.")`, or wrap a separator you don't control in `Pattern.quote(sep)` so it's matched literally.

The other behavior to know is that **trailing empty strings are dropped by default**. Splitting `"a,,b,,"` by `,` gives `["a", "", "b"]` — the empties after the last comma vanish (leading and middle empties stay). To stand out, mention the two-arg form `split(regex, limit)`: a limit of `-1` keeps every trailing empty, a positive limit caps the number of pieces with the remainder left unsplit in the last slot, and `String.join()` (Java 8) is the inverse operation.

sections.title: Input → Regex → Array: The Step split() Actually Takes
sections.content:
The mental model that prevents the dot bug: your separator is compiled into a **regex pattern** first, and only then matched against the input. ```mermaid flowchart LR IN["Input string
'a,b,c'"] --> RE["Separator as REGEX
','"] RE --> SP["split() matches
the pattern"] SP --> OUT["String array
['a', 'b', 'c']"] ``` Swap the input for `'a.b.c'` and the separator for `.` and the picture explains the bug instantly: as a regex, `.` matches *every* position, so split finds a delimiter everywhere and returns an empty array. Escaping it to `\\.` makes the regex match a literal dot.

sections.title: The Dot Bug and Other Pitfalls
split() Limit Argument Behaviour
sections.content:
| `split(regex, limit)` | Behaviour | Example on `"a,,b,,"` split by `,` |
|---|---|---|
| `split(",")` or `split(",", 0)` | Default — trailing empty strings removed | `["a", "", "b"]` (3 elements) |
| `split(",", -1)` | Keep all including trailing empty strings | `["a", "", "b", "", ""]` (5 elements) |
| `split(",", 2)` | At most 2 parts — rest stays unsplit | `["a", ",b,,"]` (2 elements) |

sections.title: The Regex Traps That Sink split()
sections.content:
- **Splitting on `.` literally** — `split(".")` treats the dot as regex "any character", matches every position, and returns an empty array. The literal-dot split is `split("\\.")`.
- **Leaving `|`, `+`, `*`, `(`, `[` unescaped** — all are regex metacharacters with their own meaning. Escape each with `\\`, or wrap the whole separator in `Pattern.quote(sep)`.
- **Expecting trailing empties to survive** — `"a,,b,,".split(",")` drops the trailing empties and returns 3 elements, not 5. Pass `-1` as the limit to keep them all.
- **Splitting in a hot loop** — `split()` compiles the regex on every call. For repeated parsing, precompile once with `Pattern.compile(regex)` and reuse its `split()`.
- **Assuming leading empties are dropped too** — only *trailing* empties are removed; a leading delimiter still yields an empty first element.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **The argument is a regex, not a literal** — `.`, `|`, `+`, `*`, `?`, `(`, `[` carry special meaning and must be escaped with `\\`.
- **The dot bug** — `split(".")` matches every character and returns an empty array; the literal-dot split is `split("\\.")`.
- **Trailing empty strings are dropped by default** — `"a,,b,,".split(",")` yields 3 elements; `split(",", -1)` keeps all 5.
- **`split(regex, n)` caps the pieces** — a positive `n` limits the array to `n` elements; the last one holds the unsplit remainder.
- **`Pattern.quote(sep)`** — escapes a whole separator you don't control, so user input never acts as a pattern.
- **`String.join(delim, parts)` is the inverse** — added in Java 8 to rebuild a String from the pieces.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The one thing that trips people up is that `split()` doesn't take a plain separator — it takes a **regular expression**. Most of the time you don't notice, because a comma or a space means nothing special in regex, so `split(",")` just works.

The trouble starts with characters that *are* metacharacters. The classic is splitting a filename on the dot: `"report.2024.pdf".split(".")` doesn't give you three pieces — `.` in regex matches any character, so it matches everything and you get back an empty array. The fix is to escape it, `split("\\.")`; same story with the pipe, plus, and star. If the separator comes from user input or config and you can't be sure, wrap it in `Pattern.quote()` so it's treated literally.

The other behavior to know is **trailing empties**. `"a,,b,,".split(",")` returns three elements, not five — Java silently drops the empties at the end. When that matters, pass `-1` as the limit to keep them, or a positive number to cap how many pieces you get with the remainder left unsplit in the last slot. The inverse operation is `String.join()`, added in Java 8. My rule is simple: if the separator is a literal character, always escape it or quote it — never trust that a character is harmless in regex.

questions.question: What is the difference between replace() and replaceAll() in Java?
questions.title: replace() vs replaceAll() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `replace(old, new)` does a **literal string** replacement — no regex. `replaceAll(regex, replacement)` takes a **regular expression** as the first argument. If you want to replace a fixed string, `replace()` is safer and faster. Use `replaceAll()` only when you actually need pattern matching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the regex vs literal distinction between these two methods.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using replaceAll() for literal replacements — if the 'old' string contains regex metacharacters like . or + it will match more than expected. replace() is always safer for literal text.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention replaceFirst(regex, replacement) which replaces only the first match. Also: in replaceAll() the replacement string itself has special meaning for $1, $2 (captured groups) and \, so literal backslashes and dollar signs need escaping there too.

sections.title: Same Name, Different Engine: Literal Text vs Regex
sections.content:
`replace()` swaps every occurrence of one piece of text for another; `replaceAll()` does the same thing, but it matches with a **regular expression** instead of literal text.

The first surprise is the naming. `replaceAll` sounds like it replaces *all* while `replace` does *one* — that's wrong. **Both replace every occurrence.** The "all" refers to nothing useful; the real distinction is how each reads its first argument.

How they differ under the hood:
- `replace(CharSequence target, CharSequence replacement)` treats `target` as a **literal** string — every character is matched exactly as typed, no regex magic.
- `replaceAll(String regex, String replacement)` compiles the first argument as a **regex**, so `.`, `+`, `*`, `?`, `|`, `(` all carry their special meanings.

This bites the moment your search text contains a metacharacter. `s.replaceAll(".", "-")` does not replace dots — it replaces *every character* with a dash, because `.` matches anything in regex. The call you wanted was `s.replace(".", "-")`.

A nuance most people miss: in `replaceAll()` the **replacement** string is special too. `$1` injects a captured group and `\` escapes, so inserting a literal `$` needs `Matcher.quoteReplacement()`. The rule of thumb: **default to `replace()`** for fixed text, and switch to `replaceAll()` only when you genuinely need a pattern — collapsing whitespace with `"\\s+"`, stripping digits with `"\\d+"`. To stand out, mention `replaceFirst()`, which applies a regex but stops after the first match.

sections.title: replace() vs replaceAll() vs replaceFirst()
sections.content:
| Method | First argument | Replaces | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `replace(old, new)` | Literal string | All occurrences | Fixed text replacement — safe default |
| `replaceAll(regex, rep)` | Regular expression | All matches | Pattern-based replacement |
| `replaceFirst(regex, rep)` | Regular expression | First match only | Replace only the first pattern match |

sections.title: Which One to Reach For: A 10-Second Decision
sections.content:
When you're about to replace text, one question settles the choice — is your search target a fixed string, or a pattern? ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Need to replace text?"] --> L["Is the target a fixed literal?"] L -->|Yes| R["replace(old, new)
safe, no escaping"] L -->|No, it is a pattern| RA["replaceAll(regex, rep)
escape metacharacters"] RA --> RF["Only the first match?
use replaceFirst(regex, rep)"] ``` The default branch is `replace()` — it can never misfire on a stray `.` or `+`. You only cross into the regex branch when you actually want pattern power, and even then `replaceFirst()` is there when one match is enough.

sections.title: When They Differ — and When to Use Each
Why replaceAll() Misfires When You Meant replace()
sections.content:
- **Using `replaceAll()` for literal text** — if the target holds `.`, `+`, `|`, or `(`, it matches far more than intended. `replace()` is the safe literal choice and needs no escaping.
- **The dot trap** — `replaceAll(".", "-")` replaces *every character*, not the dots. You meant `replace(".", "-")`, or `replaceAll("\\.", "-")` if you specifically need regex.
- **Forgetting the replacement string is special too** — `$` and `\` in the second argument of `replaceAll()` mean group references and escapes; inserting a literal `$5` needs `Matcher.quoteReplacement()`.
- **Thinking `replace()` only swaps the first match** — it replaces all occurrences, exactly like `replaceAll()`. The name difference is regex vs literal, not quantity; `replaceFirst()` is the one that stops at one.
- **Recompiling a regex every call** — repeatedly calling `replaceAll()` in a loop recompiles the pattern each time; precompile with `Pattern.compile()` and reuse the `Matcher`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`replace()` is literal, `replaceAll()` is regex** — that's the entire difference; both replace all occurrences.
- **The name `replaceAll` misleads** — it's not "all vs first"; `replace()` also replaces all. `replaceFirst()` is the one that stops after one match.
- **The dot bug** — `replaceAll(".", "-")` wipes every character; for a literal dot use `replace(".", "-")` or escape it as `"\\."`.
- **The replacement string is special in `replaceAll()`** — `$1` injects a captured group and `\` escapes; a literal `$` needs `Matcher.quoteReplacement()`.
- **Default to `replace()`** — reach for `replaceAll()` only when you truly need a pattern like `"\\s+"` or `"\\d+"`.
- **Genuine `replaceAll()` cases** — collapsing whitespace (`"\\s+"`), stripping digits (`"\\d+"`), or removing non-alphanumerics.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Both replace text and both replace every occurrence — the name `replaceAll` is a little misleading there, because `replace()` also replaces all of them. The real difference is how each reads its first argument. `replace()` takes a **literal** string where every character is matched exactly; `replaceAll()` takes a **regular expression**.

That distinction bites when your search text contains regex metacharacters. The textbook example is `"a.b.c".replaceAll(".", "-")` — you expect the dots gone, but `.` in regex matches any character, so you get a row of dashes. With `replace(".", "-")` it does exactly what you meant. So my default is `replace()` for fixed text, and I only switch to `replaceAll()` when I genuinely need a pattern — collapsing runs of whitespace with `"\\s+"`, or stripping digits with `"\\d+"`.

One subtlety worth mentioning: in `replaceAll()` the replacement string is special too — `$1` pulls in a captured group and backslash escapes, so to insert a literal dollar sign you need `Matcher.quoteReplacement()`. And if you only want the first hit, that's `replaceFirst()`. Bottom line: literal text, use `replace()`; reach for `replaceAll()` only when you actually want regex.
